# Data movement detection patterns.
# Used by per-language extractors to identify outbound calls, DB access, MQ, cache, file I/O.

categories:
  # =========================================================================
  # Outbound HTTP
  # =========================================================================
  outbound_http:
    target_type: HTTP_SERVICE
    direction: REQUEST_RESPONSE
    patterns:
      # --- Python ---
      - receiver: "requests"
        methods: ["get", "post", "put", "delete", "patch", "head", "options"]
        language: python
        mechanism: requests
      - receiver: "httpx"
        methods: ["get", "post", "put", "delete", "patch"]
        language: python
        mechanism: httpx
      - receiver: "client"
        methods: ["get", "post", "put", "delete", "patch"]
        language: python
        mechanism: httpx
      - receiver: "aiohttp"
        methods: ["get", "post", "put", "delete"]
        language: python
        mechanism: aiohttp
      - receiver: "session"
        methods: ["get", "post", "put", "delete"]
        language: python
        mechanism: aiohttp
      - receiver: "urllib"
        methods: ["urlopen", "urlretrieve"]
        language: python
        mechanism: urllib
      # --- Java ---
      - receiver: "restTemplate"
        methods: ["getForObject", "getForEntity", "postForObject", "postForEntity", "exchange", "execute", "put", "delete"]
        language: java
        mechanism: RestTemplate
      - receiver: "webClient"
        methods: ["get", "post", "put", "delete", "patch", "method"]
        language: java
        mechanism: WebClient
      - receiver: "httpClient"
        methods: ["send", "sendAsync"]
        language: java
        mechanism: HttpClient
      # --- Java Feign ---
      # Feign clients are interfaces — detected via @FeignClient annotation.
      # Actual calls look like: feignClient.getUser(id) — matched by receiver_suffix
      # --- TypeScript/JavaScript ---
      - receiver: null
        methods: ["fetch"]
        language: typescript
        mechanism: fetch
      - receiver: "axios"
        methods: ["get", "post", "put", "delete", "patch", "request"]
        language: typescript
        mechanism: axios
      - receiver: "got"
        methods: ["get", "post", "put", "delete", "patch"]
        language: typescript
        mechanism: got
      - receiver: "superagent"
        methods: ["get", "post", "put", "delete", "patch"]
        language: typescript
        mechanism: superagent
      # --- Go ---
      - receiver: "http"
        methods: ["Get", "Post", "Head", "PostForm", "NewRequest"]
        language: go
        mechanism: net/http
      - receiver: "client"
        methods: ["Do", "Get", "Post", "Head"]
        language: go
        mechanism: net/http
      # --- C# ---
      - receiver: "HttpClient"
        methods: ["GetAsync", "PostAsync", "PutAsync", "DeleteAsync", "SendAsync", "GetStringAsync", "GetStreamAsync"]
        language: csharp
        mechanism: HttpClient

  # =========================================================================
  # Database — SQL (ORM)
  # =========================================================================
  database_orm:
    target_type: DATABASE
    patterns:
      # --- Python — SQLAlchemy ---
      - receiver: "session"
        methods: ["query", "execute", "scalar", "get"]
        direction: READ
        language: python
        mechanism: SQLAlchemy
      - receiver: "session"
        methods: ["add", "add_all", "merge", "delete", "flush", "commit", "bulk_save_objects", "bulk_insert_mappings"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: python
        mechanism: SQLAlchemy
      # --- Python — Django ORM ---
      - receiver_suffix: "objects"
        methods: ["get", "filter", "exclude", "all", "first", "last", "count", "exists", "aggregate", "values", "values_list"]
        direction: READ
        language: python
        mechanism: DjangoORM
      - receiver_suffix: "objects"
        methods: ["create", "update", "delete", "bulk_create", "bulk_update", "get_or_create", "update_or_create"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: python
        mechanism: DjangoORM
      # --- Java — JPA/Hibernate ---
      - receiver_suffix: "Repository"
        methods: ["findById", "findAll", "findBy", "existsById", "count", "getById", "getReferenceById", "getOne"]
        direction: READ
        language: java
        mechanism: JPA
      - receiver_suffix: "Repository"
        methods: ["save", "saveAll", "saveAndFlush", "delete", "deleteById", "deleteAll", "deleteAllById", "flush"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: java
        mechanism: JPA
      - receiver: "entityManager"
        methods: ["find", "createQuery", "createNativeQuery", "getReference"]
        direction: READ
        language: java
        mechanism: JPA-EntityManager
      - receiver: "entityManager"
        methods: ["persist", "merge", "remove", "flush"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: java
        mechanism: JPA-EntityManager
      # --- Java — JdbcTemplate ---
      - receiver: "jdbcTemplate"
        methods: ["query", "queryForObject", "queryForList", "queryForMap", "queryForRowSet"]
        direction: READ
        language: java
        mechanism: JdbcTemplate
      - receiver: "jdbcTemplate"
        methods: ["update", "batchUpdate", "execute"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: java
        mechanism: JdbcTemplate
      # --- TypeScript — Prisma ---
      - receiver_prefix: "prisma"
        methods: ["findMany", "findFirst", "findUnique", "findUniqueOrThrow", "count", "aggregate", "groupBy"]
        direction: READ
        language: typescript
        mechanism: Prisma
      - receiver_prefix: "prisma"
        methods: ["create", "createMany", "update", "updateMany", "upsert", "delete", "deleteMany"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: typescript
        mechanism: Prisma
      # --- TypeScript — TypeORM ---
      - receiver_suffix: "Repository"
        methods: ["find", "findOne", "findOneBy", "findBy", "count", "exist"]
        direction: READ
        language: typescript
        mechanism: TypeORM
      - receiver_suffix: "Repository"
        methods: ["save", "insert", "update", "delete", "remove", "softDelete"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: typescript
        mechanism: TypeORM
      # --- Go — database/sql ---
      - receiver: "db"
        methods: ["Query", "QueryRow", "QueryContext", "QueryRowContext"]
        direction: READ
        language: go
        mechanism: database/sql
      - receiver: "db"
        methods: ["Exec", "ExecContext"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: go
        mechanism: database/sql
      # --- Go — sqlx ---
      - receiver: "db"
        methods: ["Select", "Get", "GetContext", "SelectContext", "QueryRowx", "QueryRowxContext", "Queryx", "NamedQuery"]
        direction: READ
        language: go
        mechanism: sqlx
      - receiver: "db"
        methods: ["NamedExec", "NamedExecContext", "MustExec"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: go
        mechanism: sqlx
      # --- Go — GORM ---
      - receiver: "db"
        methods: ["Find", "First", "Last", "Take", "Where", "Scan", "Count", "Pluck"]
        direction: READ
        language: go
        mechanism: GORM
      - receiver: "db"
        methods: ["Create", "Save", "Update", "Updates", "Delete"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: go
        mechanism: GORM
      # --- C# — EF Core ---
      - receiver: "context"
        methods: ["Find", "FindAsync", "Set", "FromSqlRaw", "FromSqlInterpolated"]
        direction: READ
        language: csharp
        mechanism: EFCore
      - receiver: "context"
        methods: ["Add", "AddAsync", "AddRange", "AddRangeAsync", "Update", "Remove", "RemoveRange", "SaveChanges", "SaveChangesAsync"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: csharp
        mechanism: EFCore

  # =========================================================================
  # Database — Raw SQL
  # =========================================================================
  database_raw_sql:
    target_type: DATABASE
    patterns:
      # --- Python — psycopg2 / sqlite3 ---
      - receiver: "cursor"
        methods: ["execute", "executemany", "callproc"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: python
        mechanism: psycopg2
      - receiver: "cursor"
        methods: ["fetchone", "fetchall", "fetchmany"]
        direction: READ
        language: python
        mechanism: psycopg2
      - receiver: "conn"
        methods: ["execute", "executemany"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: python
        mechanism: psycopg2
      # --- TypeScript — pg / mysql2 / knex ---
      - receiver: "pool"
        methods: ["query", "connect"]
        direction: READ
        language: typescript
        mechanism: pg
      - receiver: "client"
        methods: ["query"]
        direction: READ
        language: typescript
        mechanism: pg
      - receiver: "knex"
        methods: ["select", "where", "from", "join"]
        direction: READ
        language: typescript
        mechanism: knex
      - receiver: "knex"
        methods: ["insert", "update", "delete", "del", "truncate"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: typescript
        mechanism: knex
      - receiver: "connection"
        methods: ["query", "execute"]
        direction: READ
        language: typescript
        mechanism: mysql2

  # =========================================================================
  # Database — NoSQL
  # =========================================================================
  database_nosql:
    target_type: DATABASE
    patterns:
      # --- Python — pymongo ---
      - receiver_suffix: "collection"
        methods: ["find", "find_one", "aggregate", "count_documents", "distinct"]
        direction: READ
        language: python
        mechanism: pymongo
      - receiver_suffix: "collection"
        methods: ["insert_one", "insert_many", "update_one", "update_many", "replace_one", "delete_one", "delete_many"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: python
        mechanism: pymongo
      # --- Python — motor (async pymongo) ---
      - receiver_suffix: "collection"
        methods: ["find", "find_one", "aggregate", "count_documents"]
        direction: READ
        language: python
        mechanism: motor
      # --- Java — Spring Data MongoDB ---
      - receiver: "mongoTemplate"
        methods: ["find", "findOne", "findById", "findAll", "count", "exists", "aggregate"]
        direction: READ
        language: java
        mechanism: SpringDataMongo
      - receiver: "mongoTemplate"
        methods: ["save", "insert", "insertAll", "updateFirst", "updateMulti", "remove", "upsert"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: java
        mechanism: SpringDataMongo
      # --- TypeScript — Mongoose ---
      - receiver_suffix: "Model"
        methods: ["find", "findOne", "findById", "countDocuments", "aggregate", "distinct"]
        direction: READ
        language: typescript
        mechanism: Mongoose
      - receiver_suffix: "Model"
        methods: ["create", "insertMany", "updateOne", "updateMany", "deleteOne", "deleteMany", "findOneAndUpdate", "findOneAndDelete"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: typescript
        mechanism: Mongoose
      # --- Go — mongo-driver ---
      - receiver: "collection"
        methods: ["Find", "FindOne", "CountDocuments", "Aggregate", "Distinct"]
        direction: READ
        language: go
        mechanism: mongo-driver
      - receiver: "collection"
        methods: ["InsertOne", "InsertMany", "UpdateOne", "UpdateMany", "ReplaceOne", "DeleteOne", "DeleteMany", "FindOneAndUpdate", "FindOneAndReplace", "FindOneAndDelete"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: go
        mechanism: mongo-driver

  # =========================================================================
  # Database — Search
  # =========================================================================
  search:
    target_type: SEARCH_ENGINE
    patterns:
      # --- Python — elasticsearch-py ---
      - receiver: "es"
        methods: ["search", "get", "mget", "msearch", "count", "exists", "scroll"]
        direction: READ
        language: python
        mechanism: elasticsearch-py
      - receiver: "es"
        methods: ["index", "bulk", "update", "delete", "reindex"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: python
        mechanism: elasticsearch-py
      # --- Java — Spring Data Elasticsearch ---
      - receiver_suffix: "ElasticsearchRepository"
        methods: ["findById", "findAll", "search", "count"]
        direction: READ
        language: java
        mechanism: SpringDataElasticsearch
      - receiver_suffix: "ElasticsearchRepository"
        methods: ["save", "saveAll", "delete", "deleteAll", "deleteById"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: java
        mechanism: SpringDataElasticsearch
      - receiver: "elasticsearchOperations"
        methods: ["search", "get", "multiGet", "count", "exists"]
        direction: READ
        language: java
        mechanism: SpringDataElasticsearch
      - receiver: "elasticsearchOperations"
        methods: ["save", "bulkIndex", "delete", "update"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: java
        mechanism: SpringDataElasticsearch
      # --- TypeScript — @elastic/elasticsearch ---
      - receiver: "esClient"
        methods: ["search", "get", "mget", "msearch", "count", "exists", "scroll"]
        direction: READ
        language: typescript
        mechanism: elasticsearch-js
      - receiver: "esClient"
        methods: ["index", "bulk", "update", "delete", "reindex"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: typescript
        mechanism: elasticsearch-js
      # --- Go — olivere/elastic ---
      - receiver: "elastic"
        methods: ["Search", "Get", "MultiGet", "Count", "Exists", "Scroll"]
        direction: READ
        language: go
        mechanism: olivere-elastic
      - receiver: "elastic"
        methods: ["Index", "Bulk", "Update", "Delete", "Reindex"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: go
        mechanism: olivere-elastic

  # =========================================================================
  # Message Queue
  # =========================================================================
  message_queue:
    target_type: MESSAGE_QUEUE
    patterns:
      # --- Java ---
      - receiver: "kafkaTemplate"
        methods: ["send", "sendDefault", "sendOffsetsToTransaction"]
        direction: PUBLISH
        language: java
        mechanism: KafkaTemplate
      - receiver: "rabbitTemplate"
        methods: ["convertAndSend", "send", "convertSendAndReceive", "sendAndReceive"]
        direction: PUBLISH
        language: java
        mechanism: RabbitTemplate
      - receiver: "jmsTemplate"
        methods: ["send", "convertAndSend"]
        direction: PUBLISH
        language: java
        mechanism: JmsTemplate
      - receiver: "streamBridge"
        methods: ["send"]
        direction: PUBLISH
        language: java
        mechanism: SpringCloudStream
      # --- Python ---
      - receiver: "producer"
        methods: ["send", "produce", "send_message"]
        direction: PUBLISH
        language: python
        mechanism: kafka-python
      - receiver: "channel"
        methods: ["basic_publish", "publish"]
        direction: PUBLISH
        language: python
        mechanism: pika
      # --- Python — SQS/SNS ---
      - receiver: "sqs_client"
        methods: ["send_message", "send_message_batch"]
        direction: PUBLISH
        language: python
        mechanism: boto3-sqs
      - receiver: "sns_client"
        methods: ["publish"]
        direction: PUBLISH
        language: python
        mechanism: boto3-sns
      # --- TypeScript ---
      - receiver: "producer"
        methods: ["send", "sendBatch"]
        direction: PUBLISH
        language: typescript

# Data movement detection patterns.
# Used by per-language extractors to identify outbound calls, DB access, MQ, cache, file I/O.

categories:
  # =========================================================================
  # Outbound HTTP
  # =========================================================================
  outbound_http:
    target_type: HTTP_SERVICE
    direction: REQUEST_RESPONSE
    patterns:
      # --- Python ---
      - receiver: "requests"
        methods: ["get", "post", "put", "delete", "patch", "head", "options"]
        language: python
        mechanism: requests
      - receiver: "httpx"
        methods: ["get", "post", "put", "delete", "patch"]
        language: python
        mechanism: httpx
      - receiver: "client"
        methods: ["get", "post", "put", "delete", "patch"]
        language: python
        mechanism: httpx
      - receiver: "aiohttp"
        methods: ["get", "post", "put", "delete"]
        language: python
        mechanism: aiohttp
      - receiver: "session"
        methods: ["get", "post", "put", "delete"]
        language: python
        mechanism: aiohttp
      - receiver: "urllib"
        methods: ["urlopen", "urlretrieve"]
        language: python
        mechanism: urllib
      # --- Java ---
      - receiver: "restTemplate"
        methods: ["getForObject", "getForEntity", "postForObject", "postForEntity", "exchange", "execute", "put", "delete"]
        language: java
        mechanism: RestTemplate
      - receiver: "webClient"
        methods: ["get", "post", "put", "delete", "patch", "method"]
        language: java
        mechanism: WebClient
      - receiver: "httpClient"
        methods: ["send", "sendAsync"]
        language: java
        mechanism: HttpClient
      # --- Java Feign ---
      # Feign clients are interfaces — detected via @FeignClient annotation.
      # Actual calls look like: feignClient.getUser(id) — matched by receiver_suffix
      # --- TypeScript/JavaScript ---
      - receiver: null
        methods: ["fetch"]
        language: typescript
        mechanism: fetch
      - receiver: "axios"
        methods: ["get", "post", "put", "delete", "patch", "request"]
        language: typescript
        mechanism: axios
      - receiver: "got"
        methods: ["get", "post", "put", "delete", "patch"]
        language: typescript
        mechanism: got
      - receiver: "superagent"
        methods: ["get", "post", "put", "delete", "patch"]
        language: typescript
        mechanism: superagent
      # --- Go ---
      - receiver: "http"
        methods: ["Get", "Post", "Head", "PostForm", "NewRequest"]
        language: go
        mechanism: net/http
      - receiver: "client"
        methods: ["Do", "Get", "Post", "Head"]
        language: go
        mechanism: net/http
      # --- C# ---
      - receiver: "HttpClient"
        methods: ["GetAsync", "PostAsync", "PutAsync", "DeleteAsync", "SendAsync", "GetStringAsync", "GetStreamAsync"]
        language: csharp
        mechanism: HttpClient

  # =========================================================================
  # Database — SQL (ORM)
  # =========================================================================
  database_orm:
    target_type: DATABASE
    patterns:
      # --- Python — SQLAlchemy ---
      - receiver: "session"
        methods: ["query", "execute", "scalar", "get"]
        direction: READ
        language: python
        mechanism: SQLAlchemy
      - receiver: "session"
        methods: ["add", "add_all", "merge", "delete", "flush", "commit", "bulk_save_objects", "bulk_insert_mappings"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: python
        mechanism: SQLAlchemy
      # --- Python — Django ORM ---
      - receiver_suffix: "objects"
        methods: ["get", "filter", "exclude", "all", "first", "last", "count", "exists", "aggregate", "values", "values_list"]
        direction: READ
        language: python
        mechanism: DjangoORM
      - receiver_suffix: "objects"
        methods: ["create", "update", "delete", "bulk_create", "bulk_update", "get_or_create", "update_or_create"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: python
        mechanism: DjangoORM
      # --- Java — JPA/Hibernate ---
      - receiver_suffix: "Repository"
        methods: ["findById", "findAll", "findBy", "existsById", "count", "getById", "getReferenceById", "getOne"]
        direction: READ
        language: java
        mechanism: JPA
      - receiver_suffix: "Repository"
        methods: ["save", "saveAll", "saveAndFlush", "delete", "deleteById", "deleteAll", "deleteAllById", "flush"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: java
        mechanism: JPA
      - receiver: "entityManager"
        methods: ["find", "createQuery", "createNativeQuery", "getReference"]
        direction: READ
        language: java
        mechanism: JPA-EntityManager
      - receiver: "entityManager"
        methods: ["persist", "merge", "remove", "flush"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: java
        mechanism: JPA-EntityManager
      # --- Java — JdbcTemplate ---
      - receiver: "jdbcTemplate"
        methods: ["query", "queryForObject", "queryForList", "queryForMap", "queryForRowSet"]
        direction: READ
        language: java
        mechanism: JdbcTemplate
      - receiver: "jdbcTemplate"
        methods: ["update", "batchUpdate", "execute"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: java
        mechanism: JdbcTemplate
      # --- TypeScript — Prisma ---
      - receiver_prefix: "prisma"
        methods: ["findMany", "findFirst", "findUnique", "findUniqueOrThrow", "count", "aggregate", "groupBy"]
        direction: READ
        language: typescript
        mechanism: Prisma
      - receiver_prefix: "prisma"
        methods: ["create", "createMany", "update", "updateMany", "upsert", "delete", "deleteMany"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: typescript
        mechanism: Prisma
      # --- TypeScript — TypeORM ---
      - receiver_suffix: "Repository"
        methods: ["find", "findOne", "findOneBy", "findBy", "count", "exist"]
        direction: READ
        language: typescript
        mechanism: TypeORM
      - receiver_suffix: "Repository"
        methods: ["save", "insert", "update", "delete", "remove", "softDelete"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: typescript
        mechanism: TypeORM
      # --- Go — database/sql ---
      - receiver: "db"
        methods: ["Query", "QueryRow", "QueryContext", "QueryRowContext"]
        direction: READ
        language: go
        mechanism: database/sql
      - receiver: "db"
        methods: ["Exec", "ExecContext"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: go
        mechanism: database/sql
      # --- Go — sqlx ---
      - receiver: "db"

      - receiver: "db"

        direction: WRITE
        language: go
        mechanism: sqlx
      # --- Go — GORM ---
      - receiver: "db"
        methods: ["Find", "First", "Last", "Take", "Where", "Scan", "Count", "Pluck"]
        direction: READ
        language: go
        mechanism: GORM
      - receiver: "db"
        methods: ["Create", "Save", "Update", "Updates", "Delete"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: go
        mechanism: GORM
      # --- C# — EF Core ---
      - receiver: "context"
        methods: ["Find", "FindAsync", "Set", "FromSqlRaw", "FromSqlInterpolated"]
        direction: READ
        language: csharp
        mechanism: EFCore
      - receiver: "context"
        methods: ["Add", "AddAsync", "AddRange", "AddRangeAsync", "Update", "Remove", "RemoveRange", "SaveChanges", "SaveChangesAsync"]
        direction: WRITE

  # =========================================================================
  # Database — Raw SQL
  # =========================================================================
  database_raw_sql:
    target_type: DATABASE
    patterns:
      # --- Python — psycopg2 / sqlite3 ---
      - receiver: "cursor"
        methods: ["execute", "executemany", "callproc"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: python
        mechanism: psycopg2
      - receiver: "cursor"
        methods: ["fetchone", "fetchall", "fetchmany"]
        direction: READ
        language: python
        mechanism: psycopg2
      - receiver: "conn"
        methods: ["execute", "executemany"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: python
        mechanism: psycopg2
      # --- TypeScript — pg / mysql2 / knex ---
      - receiver: "pool"
        methods: ["query", "connect"]
        direction: READ
        language: typescript
        mechanism: pg
      - receiver: "client"
        methods: ["query"]
        direction: READ
        language: typescript
        mechanism: pg
      - receiver: "knex"
        methods: ["select", "where", "from", "join"]
        direction: READ
        language: typescript
        mechanism: knex
      - receiver: "knex"
        methods: ["insert", "update", "delete", "del", "truncate"]
        direction: WRITE
        language: typescript
        mechanism: knex
      - receiver: "connection"

        direction: READ

  # Database — NoSQL
  # =========================================================================
  database_nosql:
    target_type: DATABASE
    patterns:
      # --- Python — pymongo ---
      - receiver_suffix: "collection"

        direction: READ
        language: python
        mechanism: pymongo
      - receiver_suffix: "collection"
        methods: ["insert_one", "insert_many", "update_one", "update_many", "replace_one", "delete_one", "delete_many"]

        mechanism: pymongo
      # --- Python — motor (async pymongo) ---
      - receiver_suffix: "collection"

        direction: READ
        language: python
        mechanism: motor
      # --- Java — Spring Data MongoDB ---
      - receiver: "mongoTemplate"
        methods: ["find", "findOne", "findById", "findAll", "count", "exists", "aggregate"]
        direction: READ
        language: java

      - receiver: "mongoTemplate"

  # =========================================================================

content.text:
The problem: gRPC stub methods are service-specific (`client.Hello()`, `stub.GetFeature()`, `stub.SayHello()`). Our YAML pattern matching on method names like "Get"/"Create" doesn't work because the method names are arbitrary.

The fix: **import-aware detection**. If a file imports a gRPC package, then any call on a receiver ending in `Client`/`Stub`/`BlockingStub` is a gRPC data movement — regardless of method name.

    def _walk_grpc_calls(self, node: Node, file_path: str,
                         movements: list[DataMovementInfo], imports: list):
        """Detect gRPC stub calls: pb.ExampleClient methods, *Client/*.Stub receivers."""
        if node.type == "call_expression":
            func = node.child_by_field_name("function")
            if func and func.type == "selector_expression":
                operand = func.child_by_field_name("operand")
                field_node = func.child_by_field_name("field")
                if operand and field_node:
                    receiver = operand.text.decode("utf-8")
                    method = field_node.text.decode("utf-8")
                    # Skip common non-RPC methods

                                  "Dial", "DialContext", "NewServer", "RegisterService",
                                  "Serve", "GracefulStop", "Stop", "Wait",
                                  "Printf", "Println", "Sprintf", "Errorf"):

        """Detect gRPC stub calls: pb.ExampleClient methods, *Client/*.Stub receivers."""
        if node.type == "call_expression":

                operand = func.child_by_field_name("operand")
                field_node = func.child_by_field_name("field")

message.content: Now that you did these, let's review what you did with the YAML files. Can you explain what we did before we started doing all this work?

content.text:
The spec defined a **post-hoc store parsing** approach — scan `_index.txt` and `_calls.txt` text files after they're written to find endpoint and data movement patterns. Grep the store files for strings like `router.get` or `RestTemplate.getForObject`.

What we actually built is different. The codebase had evolved to a **per-language AST extractor model** — each language (Python, Java, TypeScript, Go, C#) has its own tree-sitter extractor that walks the full syntax tree. Instead of grepping text files after the fact, we detect endpoints and data movements **while the AST is being walked**, where we have access to decorators, annotations, arguments, receiver types, and import context.

The YAML configs (`endpoint_patterns.yaml` and `data_movement_patterns.yaml`) drive what patterns each extractor looks for. The extractors load the YAML, filter by their language, then match AST nodes against those patterns during the tree walk.

But here's the thing — the YAML approach has a fundamental assumption: **you can match a data movement by receiver name + method name**. That works for most patterns (`requests.get`, `repository.save`, `kafkaTemplate.send`). But we just proved with gRPC that it breaks when method names are arbitrary. We solved gRPC by adding **import-aware detection** directly in the extractor code, bypassing the YAML entirely.

So now we have two detection strategies:
1. **YAML-driven** — receiver + method matching (146 patterns across 14 categories)
2. **Import-aware** — check imports, then match receiver shape regardless of method name (gRPC)

The question is: should we keep expanding the YAML, or is there a better architecture here?

So we now have two detection paths:

2. **Code-driven**: import checking + receiver shape (gRPC)

# Requirements: Auto-Pattern Discovery

## Context

The endpoint & data movement extraction pipeline uses YAML config files (`endpoint_patterns.yaml`, `data_movement_patterns.yaml`) to define receiver + method name patterns for 18 frameworks and 146 data movement patterns across 5 languages. Adding new frameworks or technologies requires a human to manually write YAML entries.

The pipeline already produces `_imports.txt` (every import in the repo) and has `framework_detector.py` (60+ known framework signatures). When a repo uses a framework we don't have patterns for, we detect zero endpoints/movements for it — a silent gap.

## Goal

Automatically detect unknown frameworks and generate YAML pattern entries using an LLM, so the detection configs self-extend as new repos are analysed.

## Functional Requirements

### FR-1: Unknown Framework Detection

**FR-1.1** After extraction, compare detected framework imports (`_imports.txt`) against known patterns in `endpoint_patterns.yaml` and `data_movement_patterns.yaml`.

**FR-1.2** Identify imports that match no existing pattern — these are candidate unknown frameworks.

**FR-1.3** Filter out standard library imports, test frameworks, and utility libraries (logging, json, os) — only flag integration-relevant unknowns (web frameworks, ORMs, message queues, HTTP clients, etc.).

**FR-1.4** Score candidates by frequency — a framework imported in 20 files is more important than one imported in 1 file.

### FR-2: LLM-Powered Pattern Generation

**FR-2.1** For each unknown framework candidate, send a prompt to the LLM containing:
- The framework name and language
- Sample source snippets where it's imported and used (from the repo)
- The existing YAML pattern structure (as few-shot examples)
- Whether it's likely an endpoint source, data movement, or both

**FR-2.2** The LLM generates candidate YAML entries following the exact schema of the existing config files.

**FR-2.3** Generated entries include: receiver patterns, method names, type (REST/MQ/DB/etc.), direction, protocol, mechanism name, and confidence.

### FR-3: Validation & Merge

**FR-3.1** Validate generated YAML entries against the config schema before merging.

**FR-3.2** Re-run extraction with the new patterns on the same repo to verify they produce results.

**FR-3.3** If the new patterns detect ≥ 1 endpoint or data movement, merge them into the YAML config files.

**FR-3.4** If the new patterns detect nothing, discard them (LLM hallucinated or the framework isn't actually used for integration).

**FR-3.5** New patterns are tagged with `auto_discovered: true` and a timestamp so they can be reviewed later.

### FR-4: Feedback Loop

**FR-4.1** On subsequent runs, previously auto-discovered patterns are used automatically.

**FR-4.2** A human can review, edit, or remove auto-discovered patterns.

**FR-4.3** Track which patterns were auto-discovered vs manually authored.

## Non-Functional Requirements

### NFR-1: LLM Usage
- Should work with any LLM backend already configured in the standards-extractor (Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure)
- LLM calls should be batched — one call per unknown framework, not per file
- Total LLM cost per repo analysis should be < $0.10

### NFR-2: Performance
- Unknown framework detection (FR-1) must be deterministic and fast (< 1 second)
- LLM pattern generation (FR-2) is async and optional — extraction works without it

### NFR-3: Safety
- Auto-generated patterns must not overwrite manually authored patterns
- Auto-generated patterns are clearly marked and reviewable
- Invalid YAML is never written to config files

## Out of Scope

- Auto-detecting patterns from compiled code (bytecode, WASM)
- Generating patterns for languages not supported by tree-sitter extractors
- Training a custom model for pattern detection (we use general-purpose LLMs)
- Auto-generating import-aware detection code (like the gRPC approach) — that requires extractor code changes, not just YAML

# Requirements: LLM-Powered Interaction Classification

## Context

The structural analysis pipeline already extracts:
- `_calls.txt` — every call site in the repo (caller, receiver, method, file, line, confidence)
- `_imports.txt` — every import
- `framework_detector.py` — identifies 60+ frameworks from imports

We currently use YAML config files with 146 hand-authored receiver + method patterns to classify which calls are external interactions (HTTP, database, cache, MQ, etc.). This is brittle — every new framework requires manual YAML entries.

## Goal

Replace human-maintained pattern configs with LLM-powered classification. The AST finds all calls. The LLM decides which are external interactions and classifies them.

## Functional Requirements

### FR-1: Interaction Detection via LLM

**FR-1.1** Input to the LLM:
- `_calls.txt` — all call sites with receiver, method, file, line
- Framework detection results — what frameworks are in use
- Source file access — the LLM can read source files to resolve ambiguity

**FR-1.2** The LLM classifies each call as either:
- **Internal** — application logic, utility, framework plumbing (skip)
- **External interaction** — crosses a boundary (HTTP, database, MQ, cache, filesystem, gRPC, email, event bus, etc.)

**FR-1.3** For each external interaction, the LLM determines:
- **Type**: HTTP_SERVICE, DATABASE, MESSAGE_QUEUE, CACHE, FILE_SYSTEM, GRPC_SERVICE, EMAIL, EVENT_BUS, WEBSOCKET, GRAPHQL_SERVICE, ASYNC_JOB
- **Direction**: READ, WRITE, PUBLISH, SUBSCRIBE, REQUEST_RESPONSE
- **Mechanism**: the library/framework (e.g., RestTemplate, JPA, Celery, fetch)
- **Target**: what's being called (URL, table, topic, file path) — resolved from source if possible
- **Data entity**: what data is flowing (DTO, entity class, message type) — resolved from source if possible

**FR-1.4** The LLM works as an agent — it decides how many passes it needs. It may:
- Classify obvious calls in one pass (e.g., `requests.get` is clearly HTTP)
- Follow variable references to resolve targets (e.g., trace a URL from config)
- Read surrounding source code to determine direction (e.g., SELECT vs INSERT behind `session.execute`)

### FR-2: YAML as Optional Cache

**FR-2.1** The existing YAML patterns remain as an optional fast path. If a call matches a known YAML pattern, classify it without LLM cost.

**FR-2.2** Calls that don't match any YAML pattern are sent to the LLM for classification.

**FR-2.3** The LLM's classifications can be cached as new YAML entries in `auto_discovered_patterns.yaml` to avoid repeat LLM calls on subsequent runs.

**FR-2.4** Manual YAML patterns take precedence over auto-discovered ones.

### FR-3: Pipeline Integration

**FR-3.1** The LLM classification step runs after AST extraction, as stage 2 of the pipeline:
1. Extract (AST) — find all calls, endpoints → `_calls.txt`
2. Classify (LLM) — which calls are external interactions → `_interactions.txt`
3. Map (future) — populate architecture metamodel

**FR-3.2** Classification is gated — runs only when `classify_interactions: true` is set. Without it, the pipeline falls back to YAML-only detection (current behaviour).

**FR-3.3** Output is `_interactions.txt` — enriched version of the current `_endpoints.txt` + `_data_movements.txt`, with LLM-resolved targets and data entities.

### FR-4: Cost Control

**FR-4.1** Batch calls by framework — send all Kafka-related calls in one LLM request, not one per call site.

**FR-4.2** Skip calls the YAML already classifies (FR-2.1) — only send unknowns to the LLM.

**FR-4.3** Cache LLM results so repeat analysis of the same repo doesn't re-classify known interactions.

**FR-4.4** Target < $0.10 LLM cost per repo analysis for repos under 1,000 files.

## Non-Functional Requirements

### NFR-1: Accuracy
- LLM classification should match or exceed the YAML-based detection accuracy
- False positive rate < 5% (internal calls misclassified as external)

### NFR-2: Performance
- YAML fast-path classification: < 1 second
- LLM classification: async, does not block the AST pipeline
- Results available within 30 seconds for a typical repo

### NFR-3: LLM Backend
- Works with any configured LLM (Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure)
- Uses the existing LLMClient infrastructure in the standards-extractor

## Out of Scope

- Replacing the AST extraction pipeline (tree-sitter stays as the call site detector)
- Training a custom model for classification
- Real-time streaming classification during AST extraction
- Architecture metamodel mapping (stage 3 — separate spec)

# Requirements: Auto-Pattern Discovery

## Context

The endpoint & data movement extraction pipeline uses YAML config files (`endpoint_patterns.yaml`, `data_movement_patterns.yaml`) to define receiver + method name patterns for 18 frameworks and 146 data movement patterns across 5 languages. Adding new frameworks or technologies requires a human to manually write YAML entries.

The pipeline already produces `_imports.txt` (every import in the repo) and has `framework_detector.py` (60+ known framework signatures). When a repo uses a framework we don't have patterns for, we detect zero endpoints/movements for it — a silent gap.

## Goal

Automatically detect unknown frameworks and generate YAML pattern entries using an LLM, so the detection configs self-extend as new repos are analysed.

## Functional Requirements

### FR-1: Unknown Framework Detection

**FR-1.1** After extraction, compare detected framework imports (`_imports.txt`) against known patterns in `endpoint_patterns.yaml` and `data_movement_patterns.yaml`.

**FR-1.2** Identify imports that match no existing pattern — these are candidate unknown frameworks.

**FR-1.3** Filter out standard library imports, test frameworks, and utility libraries (logging, json, os) — only flag integration-relevant unknowns (web frameworks, ORMs, message queues, HTTP clients, etc.).

**FR-1.4** Score candidates by frequency — a framework imported in 20 files is more important than one imported in 1 file.

### FR-2: LLM-Powered Pattern Generation

**FR-2.1** For each unknown framework candidate, send a prompt to the LLM containing:
- The framework name and language
- Sample source snippets where it's imported and used (from the repo)
- The existing YAML pattern structure (as few-shot examples)
- Whether it's likely an endpoint source, data movement, or both

**FR-2.2** The LLM generates candidate YAML entries following the exact schema of the existing config files.

**FR-2.3** Generated entries include: receiver patterns, method names, type (REST/MQ/DB/etc.), direction, protocol, mechanism name, and confidence.

### FR-3: Validation & Merge

**FR-3.1** Validate generated YAML entries against the config schema before merging.

**FR-3.2** Re-run extraction with the new patterns on the same repo to verify they produce results.

**FR-3.3** If the new patterns detect ≥ 1 endpoint or data movement, merge them into the YAML config files.

**FR-3.4** If the new patterns detect nothing, discard them (LLM hallucinated or the framework isn't actually used for integration).

**FR-3.5** New patterns are tagged with `auto_discovered: true` and a timestamp so they can be reviewed later.

### FR-4: Feedback Loop

**FR-4.1** On subsequent runs, previously auto-discovered patterns are used automatically.

**FR-4.2** A human can review, edit, or remove auto-discovered patterns.

**FR-4.3** Track which patterns were auto-discovered vs manually authored.

## Non-Functional Requirements

### NFR-1: LLM Usage
- Should work with any LLM backend already configured in the standards-extractor (Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure)
- LLM calls should be batched — one call per unknown framework, not per file
- Total LLM cost per repo analysis should be < $0.10

### NFR-2: Performance
- Unknown framework detection (FR-1) must be deterministic and fast (< 1 second)
- LLM pattern generation (FR-2) is async and optional — extraction works without it

### NFR-3: Safety
- Auto-generated patterns must not overwrite manually authored patterns
- Auto-generated patterns are clearly marked and reviewable
- Invalid YAML is never written to config files

## Out of Scope

- Auto-detecting patterns from compiled code (bytecode, WASM)
- Generating patterns for languages not supported by tree-sitter extractors
- Training a custom model for pattern detection (we use general-purpose LLMs)
- Auto-generating import-aware detection code (like the gRPC approach) — that requires extractor code changes, not just YAML

# Specification: LLM-Powered Interaction Classification

## Summary

Replace human-maintained YAML pattern configs with LLM-powered classification of external interactions. The AST pipeline finds all call sites. The LLM decides which are external interactions (HTTP, database, MQ, cache, etc.) and enriches them with direction, target, and data entity information. YAML patterns remain as an optional cost-saving cache.

## Relationship to Existing Work

```
Stage 1: Extract (AST)              — DONE (this repo)
  └─ _calls.txt, _imports.txt, _endpoints.txt

Stage 2: Classify (LLM)             — THIS SPEC
  └─ _interactions.txt (enriched)

Stage 3: Map (metamodel)             — Future spec
  └─ architecture.json entities
```

## Architecture

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           Existing AST Pipeline (unchanged)           │
│                                                        │
│  _calls.txt    _imports.txt    framework_detector      │
└──────────┬──────────┬──────────────┬─────────────────┘
           │          │              │
           ▼          ▼              ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              Classification Layer                      │
│                                                        │
│  ┌─────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ YAML Fast Path   │    │ LLM Agent Classifier     │  │
│  │                   │    │                          │  │
│  │ Known patterns    │    │ 1. Receive unclassified  │  │
│  │ from config +     │───▶│    call sites            │  │
│  │ auto_discovered   │    │ 2. Batch by framework    │  │
│  │                   │    │ 3. Classify type/dir     │  │
│  │ Classifies known  │    │ 4. Read source for       │  │
│  │ Skip to output    │    │    targets + entities    │  │
│  └────────┬──────────┘    │ 5. Multi-pass if needed  │  │
���           │               └────────────┬─────────────┘  │
│           │                            │                 │
│           ▼                            ▼                 │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │              Merge + Output                      │    │
│  │                                                   │    │
│  │  _interactions.txt  — all classified interactions │    │
│  │  auto_discovered_patterns.yaml — LLM cache        │    │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
└─────���────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Classification Flow

### Step 1: Load known patterns (fast path)

Load `interaction_patterns.yaml` (manual) + `auto_discovered_patterns.yaml` (cached LLM results). For each call in `_calls.txt`, attempt to match against known patterns. Matched calls are classified immediately.

### Step 2: Batch unmatched calls by framework

Group remaining unclassified calls by the framework they belong to (using `_imports.txt` + `framework_detector` results). Calls from unknown frameworks are grouped as "unknown."

### Step 3: LLM classification

For each framework batch, send a single LLM request containing:

```
You are classifying code interactions in a {language} application using {framework}.

The following call sites were detected by static analysis. For each, determine:
1. Is this an EXTERNAL interaction (crosses a system boundary) or INTERNAL (application logic)?
2. If external, classify: type, direction, mechanism, target (if resolvable), data_entity (if resolvable)

Framework imports in this repo:
{framework_imports}

Call sites:
{calls_tsv}

For ambiguous calls, I will provide source code on request.
```

The LLM responds with classifications. For ambiguous calls, it requests source snippets — the system provides them and the LLM re-evaluates. This is the multi-pass agentic loop.

### Step 4: Source enrichment (LLM-driven)

When the LLM needs more context, it requests source code by file + line range. The system reads the file and returns the snippet. The LLM uses this to:
- Resolve string arguments (URLs, topic names, table names)
- Determine direction (read vs write)
- Identify data entities (DTO classes, message types)
- Follow variable references to config

The LLM decides when it has enough information. Typical: 1 pass for obvious calls, 2-3 passes for ambiguous ones.

### Step 5: Output + cache

- Write `_interactions.txt` — all classified interactions (YAML-matched + LLM-classified)
- Write new patterns to `auto_discovered_patterns.yaml` for future runs
- Write `_classification_meta.yaml` — stats, LLM cost, cache hit rate

## Output Format

### `_interactions.txt`

```tsv
# type	target	direction	mechanism	data_entity	source_class	source_method	file	line	confidence	classified_by
HTTP_SERVICE	http://user-service/users/	REQUEST_RESPONSE	RestTemplate	UserDTO	OrderService	getUser	OrderService.java	55	0.90	yaml
DATABASE	orders	WRITE	JPA	Order	OrderService	createOrder	OrderService.java	60	0.90	yaml
MESSAGE_QUEUE	order.created	PUBLISH	KafkaStreams	OrderEvent	OrderProcessor	process	OrderProcessor.java	88	0.85	llm
CACHE	session:user:123	READ	Lettuce	Session	AuthService	getSession	AuthService.java	34	0.80	llm
```

The `classified_by` column indicates whether the classification came from YAML (deterministic) or LLM.

### `auto_discovered_patterns.yaml`

```yaml
# Auto-discovered by LLM — do not edit manually.
# Review and promote to interaction_patterns.yaml if correct.
# Generated: 2026-04-04T14:30:00Z

patterns:
  - receiver: "kafkaStreams"
    methods: ["stream", "to", "through"]
    target_type: MESSAGE_QUEUE
    direction: PUBLISH
    language: java
    mechanism: KafkaStreams
    discovered_at: "2026-04-04T14:30:00Z"
    source_repo: "my-org/order-service"
```

## Key Design Decisions

1. **AST is the index, LLM is the reader.** The AST deterministically finds all call sites. The LLM classifies which matter. This separation means the LLM never misses a call site (AST guarantees completeness) and the AST never misclassifies (LLM handles semantics).

2. **YAML is a cache, not the source of truth.** YAML patterns exist purely to avoid LLM cost for known frameworks. If all YAML was deleted, the LLM would re-discover everything. The system degrades gracefully.

3. **LLM is an agent, not a function.** The LLM decides how many passes it needs. Some calls are obvious in one pass. Others require source reading, variable tracing, or config lookup. We don't prescribe the depth — the LLM's judgement drives it.

4. **Batch by framework for cost control.** Sending 50 Kafka calls in one request is cheaper and more accurate than 50 individual calls — the LLM has context about the framework's API.

5. **Classified_by provenance.** Every interaction records whether it was classified by YAML or LLM, enabling accuracy comparison and YAML cache improvement over time.

## Limitations

- LLM classification adds latency (5-30 seconds) and cost (< $0.10 per repo)
- LLM may hallucinate classifications for unfamiliar frameworks — validation via re-extraction mitigates this
- Source enrichment requires file access — won't work on pre-computed store files without the original repo
- Multi-pass depth is unbounded — needs a max-passes cap (default: 3) to prevent runaway cost

Right — the standards extractor is itself an agentic system. So this classification step isn't a standalone feature bolted on. It's the extraction agent doing what an agent does: using tools (AST) to gather evidence, reasoning over it (LLM), and deciding what to do next (read more source, classify, or move on).

The spec should frame this as an agent task within the existing Agent-OS lifecycle, not as a separate pipeline stage. The agent already has access to the repo, the AST output, and the LLM. Classification is just the agent interpreting what the AST found.

content.text:
The pipeline stages disappear. Instead of "stage 1 runs, then stage 2 runs, then stage 3 runs," the agent gets a goal: "classify all external interactions in this repo." It has tools — AST extraction, file reading, framework detection. It decides the order, depth, and strategy.

Practically, the spec changes from describing a fixed pipeline to describing **agent capabilities and goals**:

- **Goal**: produce `_interactions.txt` for this repo
- **Tools available**: run tree-sitter, read `_calls.txt`, read source files, query framework detector, read/write YAML cache
- **Strategy**: up to the agent — it might start with YAML cache for speed, then LLM-classify the rest, or it might skip the cache entirely and classify everything from scratch

The implementation change: instead of a `ClassificationPipeline` class with hardcoded steps, you'd have an agent skill (`classify-interactions`) that gets injected into Claude with the tools and the goal. The agent's reasoning replaces our orchestration code.

The fixed code shrinks to just the tools (AST extractor, file reader, YAML loader/writer). The decision-making moves to the agent prompt.

This also means the multi-pass enrichment isn't a feature we build — it's just the agent naturally reading more files when it needs to. We don't need a "max passes" config because the agent manages its own depth.

message.content: But in the skill itself, why can't we just create a diagram to show the the pipeline procedure work iterations where applicable?

content.text:
You can. The skill prompt describes the procedure — including where to iterate. The agent follows it but uses judgement within each step. It's not "do whatever you want," it's "here's the playbook, loop where needed."

```
classify-interactions skill:

1. Run AST extraction → _calls.txt
2. Load YAML cache → classify known patterns
3. For each unclassified framework batch:
   a. Read call sites
   b. Classify type/direction
   c. If ambiguous → read source → reclassify
   d. Repeat (c) until resolved or max depth
4. Write _interactions.txt
5. Cache new patterns to auto_discovered_patterns.yaml
```

Step 3c-3d is the iteration loop. The diagram shows it as a loop. The agent executes it. The skill prompt is the procedure, the diagram documents it, the agent is the runtime.

That's how the other Agent-OS skills work already — shape-spec has a multi-phase procedure with a mandatory stop-and-ask loop in phase 2. Same pattern here.

# Specification: LLM-Powered Interaction Classification

## Summary

Replace human-maintained YAML pattern configs with LLM-powered classification of external interactions. The AST pipeline finds all call sites. The LLM decides which are external interactions (HTTP, database, MQ, cache, etc.) and enriches them with direction, target, and data entity information. YAML patterns remain as an optional cost-saving cache.

## Relationship to Existing Work

```
Stage 1: Extract (AST)              — DONE (this repo)
  └─ _calls.txt, _imports.txt, _endpoints.txt

Stage 2: Classify (LLM)             — THIS SPEC
  └─ _interactions.txt (enriched)

Stage 3: Map (metamodel)             — Future spec
  └─ architecture.json entities
```

## Architecture

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           Existing AST Pipeline (unchanged)           │
│                                                        │
│  _calls.txt    _imports.txt    framework_detector      │
└──────────┬──────────┬──────────────┬─────────────────┘
           │          │              │
           ▼          ▼              ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              Classification Layer                      │
│                                                        │
│  ┌─────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ YAML Fast Path   │    │ LLM Agent Classifier     │  │
│  │                   │    │                          │  │
│  │ Known patterns    │    │ 1. Receive unclassified  │  │
│  │ from config +     │───▶│    call sites            │  │
│  │ auto_discovered   │    │ 2. Batch by framework    │  │
│  │                   │    │ 3. Classify type/dir     │  │
│  │ Classifies known  │    │ 4. Read source for       │  │
│  │ Skip to output    │    │    targets + entities    │  │
│  └────────┬──────────┘    │ 5. Multi-pass if needed  │  │
���           │               └────────────┬─────────────┘  │
│           │                            │                 │
│           ▼                            ▼                 │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │              Merge + Output                      │    │
│  │                                                   │    │
│  │  _interactions.txt  — all classified interactions │    │
│  │  auto_discovered_patterns.yaml — LLM cache        │    │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
└─────���────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Classification Flow

### Step 1: Load known patterns (fast path)

Load `interaction_patterns.yaml` (manual) + `auto_discovered_patterns.yaml` (cached LLM results). For each call in `_calls.txt`, attempt to match against known patterns. Matched calls are classified immediately.

### Step 2: Batch unmatched calls by framework

Group remaining unclassified calls by the framework they belong to (using `_imports.txt` + `framework_detector` results). Calls from unknown frameworks are grouped as "unknown."

### Step 3: LLM classification

For each framework batch, send a single LLM request containing:

```
You are classifying code interactions in a {language} application using {framework}.

The following call sites were detected by static analysis. For each, determine:
1. Is this an EXTERNAL interaction (crosses a system boundary) or INTERNAL (application logic)?
2. If external, classify: type, direction, mechanism, target (if resolvable), data_entity (if resolvable)

Framework imports in this repo:
{framework_imports}

Call sites:
{calls_tsv}

For ambiguous calls, I will provide source code on request.
```

The LLM responds with classifications. For ambiguous calls, it requests source snippets — the system provides them and the LLM re-evaluates. This is the multi-pass agentic loop.

### Step 4: Source enrichment (LLM-driven)

When the LLM needs more context, it requests source code by file + line range. The system reads the file and returns the snippet. The LLM uses this to:
- Resolve string arguments (URLs, topic names, table names)
- Determine direction (read vs write)
- Identify data entities (DTO classes, message types)
- Follow variable references to config

The LLM decides when it has enough information. Typical: 1 pass for obvious calls, 2-3 passes for ambiguous ones.

### Step 5: Output + cache

- Write `_interactions.txt` — all classified interactions (YAML-matched + LLM-classified)
- Write new patterns to `auto_discovered_patterns.yaml` for future runs
- Write `_classification_meta.yaml` — stats, LLM cost, cache hit rate

## Output Format

### `_interactions.txt`

```tsv
# type	target	direction	mechanism	data_entity	source_class	source_method	file	line	confidence	classified_by
HTTP_SERVICE	http://user-service/users/	REQUEST_RESPONSE	RestTemplate	UserDTO	OrderService	getUser	OrderService.java	55	0.90	yaml
DATABASE	orders	WRITE	JPA	Order	OrderService	createOrder	OrderService.java	60	0.90	yaml
MESSAGE_QUEUE	order.created	PUBLISH	KafkaStreams	OrderEvent	OrderProcessor	process	OrderProcessor.java	88	0.85	llm
CACHE	session:user:123	READ	Lettuce	Session	AuthService	getSession	AuthService.java	34	0.80	llm
```

The `classified_by` column indicates whether the classification came from YAML (deterministic) or LLM.

### `auto_discovered_patterns.yaml`

```yaml
# Auto-discovered by LLM — do not edit manually.
# Review and promote to interaction_patterns.yaml if correct.
# Generated: 2026-04-04T14:30:00Z

patterns:
  - receiver: "kafkaStreams"
    methods: ["stream", "to", "through"]
    target_type: MESSAGE_QUEUE
    direction: PUBLISH
    language: java
    mechanism: KafkaStreams
    discovered_at: "2026-04-04T14:30:00Z"
    source_repo: "my-org/order-service"
```

## Key Design Decisions

1. **AST is the index, LLM is the reader.** The AST deterministically finds all call sites. The LLM classifies which matter. This separation means the LLM never misses a call site (AST guarantees completeness) and the AST never misclassifies (LLM handles semantics).

2. **YAML is a cache, not the source of truth.** YAML patterns exist purely to avoid LLM cost for known frameworks. If all YAML was deleted, the LLM would re-discover everything. The system degrades gracefully.

3. **LLM is an agent, not a function.** The LLM decides how many passes it needs. Some calls are obvious in one pass. Others require source reading, variable tracing, or config lookup. We don't prescribe the depth — the LLM's judgement drives it.

4. **Batch by framework for cost control.** Sending 50 Kafka calls in one request is cheaper and more accurate than 50 individual calls — the LLM has context about the framework's API.

5. **Classified_by provenance.** Every interaction records whether it was classified by YAML or LLM, enabling accuracy comparison and YAML cache improvement over time.

## Limitations

- LLM classification adds latency (5-30 seconds) and cost (< $0.10 per repo)
- LLM may hallucinate classifications for unfamiliar frameworks — validation via re-extraction mitigates this
- Source enrichment requires file access — won't work on pre-computed store files without the original repo
- Multi-pass depth is unbounded — needs a max-passes cap (default: 3) to prevent runaway cost

# Requirements: LLM-Powered Interaction Classification

## Context

The structural analysis pipeline already extracts:
- `_calls.txt` — every call site in the repo (caller, receiver, method, file, line, confidence)
- `_imports.txt` — every import
- `framework_detector.py` — identifies 60+ frameworks from imports

We currently use YAML config files with 146 hand-authored receiver + method patterns to classify which calls are external interactions (HTTP, database, cache, MQ, etc.). This is brittle — every new framework requires manual YAML entries.

## Goal

Replace human-maintained pattern configs with LLM-powered classification. The AST finds all calls. The LLM decides which are external interactions and classifies them.

## Functional Requirements

### FR-1: Interaction Detection via LLM

**FR-1.1** Input to the LLM:
- `_calls.txt` — all call sites with receiver, method, file, line
- Framework detection results — what frameworks are in use
- Source file access — the LLM can read source files to resolve ambiguity

**FR-1.2** The LLM classifies each call as either:
- **Internal** — application logic, utility, framework plumbing (skip)
- **External interaction** — crosses a boundary (HTTP, database, MQ, cache, filesystem, gRPC, email, event bus, etc.)

**FR-1.3** For each external interaction, the LLM determines:
- **Type**: HTTP_SERVICE, DATABASE, MESSAGE_QUEUE, CACHE, FILE_SYSTEM, GRPC_SERVICE, EMAIL, EVENT_BUS, WEBSOCKET, GRAPHQL_SERVICE, ASYNC_JOB
- **Direction**: READ, WRITE, PUBLISH, SUBSCRIBE, REQUEST_RESPONSE
- **Mechanism**: the library/framework (e.g., RestTemplate, JPA, Celery, fetch)
- **Target**: what's being called (URL, table, topic, file path) — resolved from source if possible
- **Data entity**: what data is flowing (DTO, entity class, message type) — resolved from source if possible

**FR-1.4** The LLM works as an agent — it decides how many passes it needs. It may:
- Classify obvious calls in one pass (e.g., `requests.get` is clearly HTTP)
- Follow variable references to resolve targets (e.g., trace a URL from config)
- Read surrounding source code to determine direction (e.g., SELECT vs INSERT behind `session.execute`)

### FR-2: YAML as Optional Cache

**FR-2.1** The existing YAML patterns remain as an optional fast path. If a call matches a known YAML pattern, classify it without LLM cost.

**FR-2.2** Calls that don't match any YAML pattern are sent to the LLM for classification.

**FR-2.3** The LLM's classifications can be cached as new YAML entries in `auto_discovered_patterns.yaml` to avoid repeat LLM calls on subsequent runs.

**FR-2.4** Manual YAML patterns take precedence over auto-discovered ones.

### FR-3: Pipeline Integration

**FR-3.1** The LLM classification step runs after AST extraction, as stage 2 of the pipeline:
1. Extract (AST) — find all calls, endpoints → `_calls.txt`
2. Classify (LLM) — which calls are external interactions → `_interactions.txt`
3. Map (future) — populate architecture metamodel

**FR-3.2** Classification is gated — runs only when `classify_interactions: true` is set. Without it, the pipeline falls back to YAML-only detection (current behaviour).

**FR-3.3** Output is `_interactions.txt` — enriched version of the current `_endpoints.txt` + `_data_movements.txt`, with LLM-resolved targets and data entities.

### FR-4: Cost Control

**FR-4.1** Batch calls by framework — send all Kafka-related calls in one LLM request, not one per call site.

**FR-4.2** Skip calls the YAML already classifies (FR-2.1) — only send unknowns to the LLM.

**FR-4.3** Cache LLM results so repeat analysis of the same repo doesn't re-classify known interactions.

**FR-4.4** Target < $0.10 LLM cost per repo analysis for repos under 1,000 files.

## Non-Functional Requirements

### NFR-1: Accuracy
- LLM classification should match or exceed the YAML-based detection accuracy
- False positive rate < 5% (internal calls misclassified as external)

### NFR-2: Performance
- YAML fast-path classification: < 1 second
- LLM classification: async, does not block the AST pipeline
- Results available within 30 seconds for a typical repo

### NFR-3: LLM Backend
- Works with any configured LLM (Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure)
- Uses the existing LLMClient infrastructure in the standards-extractor

## Out of Scope

- Replacing the AST extraction pipeline (tree-sitter stays as the call site detector)
- Training a custom model for classification
- Real-time streaming classification during AST extraction
- Architecture metamodel mapping (stage 3 — separate spec)

# Specification: LLM-Powered Interaction Classification

## Summary

Replace human-maintained YAML pattern configs with LLM-powered classification of external interactions. The AST pipeline finds all call sites. An LLM agent classifies which are external interactions and enriches them with direction, target, and data entity information. YAML patterns remain as an optional cost-saving cache.

## Relationship to Existing Work

```
Stage 1: Extract (AST)              — DONE (this repo)
  └─ _calls.txt, _imports.txt, _endpoints.txt

Stage 2: Classify (LLM agent)       — THIS SPEC
  └─ _interactions.txt (enriched)

Stage 3: Map (metamodel)             — Future spec
  └─ architecture.json entities
```

## Architecture

See [classification-flow.dot](planning/visuals/classification-flow.dot) for the Graphviz diagram of the full procedure including iteration loops.

Render with: `dot -Tpng planning/visuals/classification-flow.dot -o planning/visuals/classification-flow.png`

## Agent Skill: `classify-interactions`

This is an Agent-OS skill. The agent has a goal, tools, and a procedure. It uses judgement within each step — including deciding iteration depth.

**Goal:** Produce `_interactions.txt` — every external interaction in the repo, classified and enriched.

**Tools available:**
- Read `_calls.txt` (all call sites from AST)
- Read `_imports.txt` (all imports)
- Query `framework_detector` (identified frameworks)
- Read source files (for enrichment)
- Read/write YAML cache (`interaction_patterns.yaml`, `auto_discovered_patterns.yaml`)

## Classification Flow

### Step 1: Load known patterns (fast path)

Load `interaction_patterns.yaml` (manual) + `auto_discovered_patterns.yaml` (cached LLM results). For each call in `_calls.txt`, attempt to match against known patterns. Matched calls are classified immediately.

### Step 2: Batch unmatched calls by framework

Group remaining unclassified calls by the framework they belong to (using `_imports.txt` + `framework_detector` results). Calls from unknown frameworks are grouped as "unknown."

### Step 3: LLM classification

For each framework batch, the agent classifies call sites:

1. Is this an **external interaction** (crosses a system boundary) or **internal** (application logic)?
2. If external: type, direction, mechanism

The agent receives call sites as AST data (receiver, method, file, line). For obvious patterns (e.g., `requests.get`) it classifies immediately.

### Step 4: Source enrichment (iterative)

For ambiguous calls, the agent reads the source code around the call site. It uses this to:
- Resolve string arguments (URLs, topic names, table names)
- Determine direction (read vs write)
- Identify data entities (DTO classes, message types)
- Follow variable references to config

The agent decides when it has enough information. It may make multiple passes — following a variable from a call site to its definition to a config file. Typical: 1 pass for obvious calls, 2-3 for ambiguous ones.

### Step 5: Output + cache

- Write `_interactions.txt` — all classified interactions (YAML-matched + LLM-classified)
- Write new patterns to `auto_discovered_patterns.yaml` for future runs
- Write `_classification_meta.yaml` — stats, LLM cost, cache hit rate

## Output Format

### `_interactions.txt`

```tsv
# type	target	direction	mechanism	data_entity	source_class	source_method	file	line	confidence	classified_by
HTTP_SERVICE	http://user-service/users/	REQUEST_RESPONSE	RestTemplate	UserDTO	OrderService	getUser	OrderService.java	55	0.90	yaml
DATABASE	orders	WRITE	JPA	Order	OrderService	createOrder	OrderService.java	60	0.90	yaml
MESSAGE_QUEUE	order.created	PUBLISH	KafkaStreams	OrderEvent	OrderProcessor	process	OrderProcessor.java	88	0.85	llm
CACHE	session:user:123	READ	Lettuce	Session	AuthService	getSession	AuthService.java	34	0.80	llm
```

The `classified_by` column indicates whether the classification came from YAML (deterministic) or LLM.

### `auto_discovered_patterns.yaml`

```yaml
# Auto-discovered by LLM — do not edit manually.
# Review and promote to interaction_patterns.yaml if correct.
# Generated: 2026-04-04T14:30:00Z

patterns:
  - receiver: "kafkaStreams"
    methods: ["stream", "to", "through"]
    target_type: MESSAGE_QUEUE
    direction: PUBLISH
    language: java
    mechanism: KafkaStreams
    discovered_at: "2026-04-04T14:30:00Z"
    source_repo: "my-org/order-service"
```

## Key Design Decisions

1. **AST is the index, LLM is the reader.** The AST deterministically finds all call sites. The LLM classifies which matter. The LLM never misses a call (AST guarantees completeness). The AST never misclassifies (LLM handles semantics).

2. **YAML is a cache, not the source of truth.** YAML patterns avoid LLM cost for known frameworks. If all YAML was deleted, the LLM would re-discover everything. The system degrades gracefully.

3. **LLM is an agent, not a function.** It decides how many passes it needs. Some calls are obvious in one pass. Others require source reading, variable tracing, or config lookup. The procedure (Graphviz diagram) shows where iteration happens — the agent decides the depth.

4. **Batch by framework for cost control.** Sending 50 Kafka calls in one request is cheaper and more accurate than 50 individual requests.

5. **Classified_by provenance.** Every interaction records whether it was classified by YAML or LLM, enabling accuracy comparison and cache improvement over time.

## Limitations

- LLM classification adds latency (5-30 seconds) and cost (< $0.10 per repo)
- LLM may hallucinate classifications — validation via re-extraction mitigates this
- Source enrichment requires file access — won't work on pre-computed store files without the original repo
- Multi-pass depth needs a cap (default: 3) to prevent runaway cost

"""Config loader for endpoint and data movement detection patterns.

Reads YAML configs and provides pattern lookup by language/framework.
Follows the same pattern as treesitter_config.py.
"""
import logging
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Optional

import yaml

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

ENDPOINT_CONFIG_PATH = "config/endpoint_patterns.yaml"
DATA_MOVEMENT_CONFIG_PATH = "config/data_movement_patterns.yaml"

_endpoint_cache: Optional[dict] = None
_data_movement_cache: Optional[dict] = None


def load_endpoint_patterns(config_path: Optional[str] = None) -> dict:
    """Load endpoint detection patterns from YAML.

    Returns:
        Dict keyed by framework name, each containing language + detection rules.
    """
    global _endpoint_cache
    if _endpoint_cache is not None:
        return _endpoint_cache

    path = config_path or ENDPOINT_CONFIG_PATH
    try:
        with open(path) as f:
            raw = yaml.safe_load(f) or {}
        _endpoint_cache = raw.get("frameworks", {})
    except FileNotFoundError:
        logger.warning(f"Endpoint patterns config not found: {path}")
        _endpoint_cache = {}
    except Exception as e:
        logger.warning(f"Endpoint patterns config error: {e}")
        _endpoint_cache = {}

    return _endpoint_cache


def load_data_movement_patterns(config_path: Optional[str] = None) -> dict:
    """Load data movement detection patterns from YAML.

    Returns:
        Dict keyed by category (outbound_http, database, message_queue, cache, file_system).
    """
    global _data_movement_cache
    if _data_movement_cache is not None:
        return _data_movement_cache

    path = config_path or DATA_MOVEMENT_CONFIG_PATH
    try:
        with open(path) as f:
            raw = yaml.safe_load(f) or {}
        _data_movement_cache = raw.get("categories", {})
    except FileNotFoundError:
        logger.warning(f"Data movement patterns config not found: {path}")
        _data_movement_cache = {}
    except Exception as e:
        logger.warning(f"Data movement patterns config error: {e}")
        _data_movement_cache = {}

    return _data_movement_cache


def get_endpoint_frameworks(language: str, config_path: Optional[str] = None) -> dict:
    """Get endpoint detection rules for a specific language.

    Returns:
        Dict of framework_name -> rules, filtered to the given language.
    """
    all_patterns = load_endpoint_patterns(config_path)
    return {
        name: config
        for name, config in all_patterns.items()
        if config.get("language") == language
    }


def get_data_movement_patterns(language: str, config_path: Optional[str] = None) -> list[dict]:
    """Get data movement patterns for a specific language.

    Returns:
        Flat list of pattern dicts, each with target_type, direction, receiver, methods, mechanism.
    """
    all_categories = load_data_movement_patterns(config_path)
    results = []

"""Tree-sitter based call graph extraction.

Config-driven multi-language provider. Routes files to the correct
language extractor based on file extension, then resolves call targets
using the shared 5-stage resolution pipeline.

Architecture:
    config/treesitter_languages.yaml  → extension → extractor mapping
    src/ast/extractors/*.py           → per-language AST walking
    src/ast/treesitter_resolver.py    → language-agnostic resolution
    src/ast/treesitter_utils.py       → index/import file parsing
"""
import logging
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Optional

from src.ast.models import StructuralAnalysis, ImportInfo, EndpointInfo, DataMovementInfo
from src.ast.provider import AnalysisProvider
from src.ast.treesitter_models import RawCallSite, ResolutionContext
from src.ast.treesitter_resolver import CallResolver
from src.ast.treesitter_utils import parse_index, parse_imports
from src.ast.treesitter_config import load_extractors

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


class TreeSitterProvider(AnalysisProvider):
    """Config-driven call graph extraction via tree-sitter AST parsing.

    Routes files to per-language extractors, merges raw call sites,
    then resolves all calls through the shared pipeline.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        index_path: Optional[str] = None,
        imports_path: Optional[str] = None,
        config_path: Optional[str] = None,
    ):
        self._index_path = index_path
        self._imports_path = imports_path
        self._resolver = CallResolver()
        self._extractors = load_extractors(config_path)

    @property
    def name(self) -> str:
        return "treesitter"

    def is_available(self) -> bool:
        return len(self._extractors) > 0

    def analyze_batch(self, file_paths: list[str]) -> dict[str, StructuralAnalysis]:
        """Parse all files, extract calls, resolve targets.

        Groups files by extension, routes to correct extractor,
        then resolves all calls through the shared pipeline.
        """
        # Group files by extractor
        grouped: dict[str, list[str]] = {}
        for fp in file_paths:
            ext = Path(fp).suffix
            if ext in self._extractors:
                grouped.setdefault(ext, []).append(fp)

        if not grouped:
            return {}

        # Phase 1: Extract raw data from all files using per-language extractors
        all_calls: dict[str, list[RawCallSite]] = {}
        all_assignments: dict[str, str] = {}
        all_annotations: dict[str, str] = {}
        all_imports: dict[str, list[ImportInfo]] = {}
        all_endpoints: dict[str, list[EndpointInfo]] = {}
        all_data_movements: dict[str, list[DataMovementInfo]] = {}
        file_languages: dict[str, str] = {}

        for ext, files in grouped.items():
            extractor = self._extractors[ext]
            for fp in files:
                try:
                    source = Path(fp).read_bytes()
                except Exception:
                    continue

                calls = extractor.extract_calls(source, fp)
                if calls:
                    all_calls[fp] = calls

                assignments = extractor.extract_assignments(source)
                all_assignments.update(assignments)

                annotations = extractor.extract_annotations(source)
                all_annotations.update(annotations)

                raw_imports = extractor.extract_imports(source)
                if raw_imports:
                    all_imports[fp] = [
                        ImportInfo(module=module, names=names, is_relative=is_rel)
                        for module, names, is_rel in raw_imports
                    ]

                endpoints = extractor.extract_endpoints(source, fp)
                if endpoints:
                    all_endpoints[fp] = endpoints

                data_movements = extractor.extract_data_movements(source, fp)
                if data_movements:
                    all_data_movements[fp] = data_movements

                # Track language per file (derive from extension)
                file_languages[fp] = ext.lstrip(".")

        # Phase 2: Build resolution context
        context = ResolutionContext(
            assignments=all_assignments,
            annotations=all_annotations,
        )

        if self._index_path:
            context.symbol_index, context.class_index = parse_index(self._index_path)

        if self._imports_path:
            context.imports = parse_imports(self._imports_path)

        # Phase 3: Resolve each call
        all_analyzed_files = []
        for files in grouped.values():
            all_analyzed_files.extend(files)

        results: dict[str, StructuralAnalysis] = {}
        for fp in all_analyzed_files:
            raw = all_calls.get(fp, [])
            resolved = [self._resolver.resolve(c, context) for c in raw]

            # Map extension to language name
            lang = file_languages.get(fp, "unknown")
            lang_map = {"py": "python", "pyi": "python", "ts": "typescript",
                        "tsx": "typescript", "js": "javascript", "jsx": "javascript",
                        "go": "go"}

            results[fp] = StructuralAnalysis(
                file_path=fp,
                language=lang_map.get(lang, lang),
                imports=all_imports.get(fp, []),
                calls=resolved,
                endpoints=all_endpoints.get(fp, []),
                data_movements=all_data_movements.get(fp, []),
                provider_used="treesitter",
                analysis_depth="rich",
            )

        total_calls = sum(len(a.calls) for a in results.values())
        total_eps = sum(len(a.endpoints) for a in results.values())
        total_dms = sum(len(a.data_movements) for a in results.values())
        if total_calls or total_eps:
            logger.info(
                f"Tree-sitter: {len(results)} files, {total_calls} call edges, "
                f"{total_eps} endpoints, {total_dms} data movements"
            )

        return results
